job_boxesCeil.prompt: ${n}$ parts are packed ${k}$ to a box, and boxes are stacked ${m}$ to a pallet for transport. A leftover part still goes into a box of its own, and leftover boxes still go onto a pallet. What is the smallest number of pallets needed? (digits only)
hints: If the division is not exact, one more box (pallet) is needed for the remainder.
Find the number of boxes first, then the number of pallets in the same way.
job_boxesCeil.expl: The number of boxes is ${n}\div{k}$ rounded up, ${bx}$; the number of pallets is ${bx}\div{m}$ rounded up, ${ans}$.

job_ratioChain.prompt: Three processes A, B, C have daily outputs in the ratios A : B $={a}:{b}$ and B : C $={c}:{d}$. The total daily output of the three is ${T}$ items. How many items does process C make per day? (digits only)
hints: Use B as the link to join the two ratios into one ratio A : B : C.
Divide the total ${T}$ by the sum of the parts of A : B : C to get the size of one part.
job_ratioChain.expl: Matching the value of B gives A : B : C $={pa}:{pb}:{pc}$. The parts sum to ${S}$, so one part is ${T}\div{S}={u}$ items and C makes ${pc}\times{u}={ans}$ items.

job_markupProfit.prompt: A shop sets the list price of an item costing ${c}$ won by adding ${u}$% of the cost as margin, then sells all ${n}$ items at ${d}$% off the list price. What is the total profit over the cost, in won? (digits only)
hints: The list price is $(100+{u})$% of the cost.
The selling price is $(100-{d})$% of the list price, and the profit per item is (selling price)−(cost).
job_markupProfit.expl: The list price is ${c}\times\frac{{100+u}}{100}={lp}$ won and the selling price is ${lp}\times\frac{{100-d}}{100}={sp}$ won. The profit per item is ${sp}-{c}={g}$ won, so for ${n}$ items it is ${g}\times{n}={ans}$ won.

job_tableRule.prompt: Here is the rental price list of a machine. For each extra hour, the price increases by the same amount. ${x1}$ hours cost ${y1}$ won, ${x2}$ hours cost ${y2}$ won and ${x3}$ hours cost ${y3}$ won. What is the price for ${N}$ hours, in won? (digits only)
hints: From the table, find how much the price rises per extra hour.
Write the price as (increase per hour)×(hours)+(base amount) and find the base amount.
job_tableRule.expl: The price rises by ${k}$ won per hour, so $y={k}x+{b}$ (the base amount ${b}$ won makes ${x1}$ hours cost ${y1}$ won). For ${N}$ hours: ${k}\times{N}+{b}={ans}$ won.

job_planCompare.prompt: Plan A costs a monthly fee of ${f1}$ won plus ${p1}$ won per use; plan B costs a monthly fee of ${f2}$ won plus ${p2}$ won per use. If you use the service $x$ times a month ($x$ is a natural number), what is the smallest $x$ for which plan B's monthly cost is lower than plan A's? (digits only)
hints: Write the monthly cost of each plan as an expression in $x$.
Solve the inequality (cost of B) < (cost of A) for $x$.
job_planCompare.expl: Plan A costs ${f1}+{p1}x$ and plan B costs ${f2}+{p2}x$. From ${f2}+{p2}x<{f1}+{p1}x$ we get ${dl}x>{df}$, i.e. $x>\frac{{df}}{{dl}}$. The smallest natural number satisfying this is ${ans}$.

job_workTogether.prompt: Worker A makes ${a}$ items per hour and worker B makes ${b}$ items per hour, each at a constant speed. A starts first and B joins ${h}$ hours later. How many hours has A worked in total when the two together have made exactly ${N}$ items? (digits only)
hints: If A has worked $t$ hours, B has worked $t-{h}$ hours.
Set up the linear equation (items by A)+(items by B)$={N}$.
job_workTogether.expl: If A works $t$ hours, B works $t-{h}$ hours, so ${a}t+{b}(t-{h})={N}$. This simplifies to ${ab}t={tot}$, so $t={ans}$ hours.

job_floorPlan.prompt: A rectangular room is ${a}$ m wide and ${b}$ m deep. A rectangular alcove ${d}$ m wide and ${c}$ m deep is attached outward in the middle of one of the walls of length ${a}$ (${d}<{a}$, and it does not touch the corners of the room). Skirting board is fixed along the whole inner wall, except for a door opening ${w}$ m wide. How many metres of skirting board are needed? (digits only)
hints: Sketch the shape and compare its perimeter with that of the plain rectangle.
The wall of length ${d}$ m is replaced by two sides of ${c}$ m and one side of ${d}$ m.
job_floorPlan.expl: The whole perimeter is $2({a}+{b})+2\times{c}={per}$ m (the side of length ${d}$ is replaced by two sides of ${c}$ and one of ${d}$, so only the two sides of ${c}$ m are added). Subtracting the door ${w}$ m gives ${per}-{w}={ans}$ m.

job_boxTunnel.prompt: A wooden block is a rectangular box ${a}$ cm long, ${b}$ cm wide and ${c}$ cm high. A rectangular hole ${p}$ cm by ${q}$ cm is drilled straight from the middle of the top face to the bottom face (the hole does not touch the side faces of the block). Counting the inner walls of the hole as part of the surface, what is the surface area of the block in cm²? (digits only)
hints: Drilling removes a rectangle of the hole's cross-section from both the top and the bottom face.
On the other hand, four new inner side faces appear.
job_boxTunnel.expl: Before drilling, the surface area is $2({a}\times{b}+{b}\times{c}+{c}\times{a})={s0}$ cm². Subtract ${p}\times{q}$ twice for the top and bottom, and add the inner walls $2({p}+{q})\times{c}$: ${s0}-{pq2}+{inn}={ans}$ cm².

job_scaleDrawing.prompt: On a drawing with scale $1:{k}$, a rectangular room is drawn ${w}$ cm long and ${h}$ cm wide. What is the actual floor area of the room in m²? (1 m = 100 cm. Digits only.)
hints: With scale $1:{k}$, multiplying a length on the drawing by ${k}$ gives the actual length.
Find the actual length and width in cm, convert them to m, and multiply.
job_scaleDrawing.expl: The actual length is ${w}\times{k}={rw}$ cm $={rwm}$ m and the actual width is ${h}\times{k}={rh}$ cm $={rhm}$ m, so the area is ${rwm}\times{rhm}={ans}$ m².

job_outfitCount.prompt: There are ${s}$ work tops, ${p}$ work bottoms and ${h}$ hats. One top and one bottom are chosen, and one of the ${h}$ hats may be worn or no hat at all. If ${f}$ (top, bottom) pairs may not be worn together for safety reasons, how many different outfits are possible? (digits only)
hints: First count the allowed (top, bottom) pairs.
Count the hat choices, including wearing no hat, and multiply.
job_outfitCount.expl: The allowed (top, bottom) pairs number ${s}\times{p}-{f}={ok}$; the hat choices, including no hat, number ${h}+1={hh}$. By the product rule, ${ok}\times{hh}={ans}$.

job_chanceDraw.prompt: A box holds ${n}$ parts, of which ${d}$ are defective. Two parts are drawn at random at the same time. What is the probability that at least one of them is defective? (a decimal or a fraction like 3/4 is fine)
hints: The number of all possible draws is the number of ways to choose 2 out of ${n}$.
The opposite of 'at least one defective' is 'both are good'.
job_chanceDraw.expl: There are $_{{n}}\mathrm{C}_{2}={tot}$ draws in all, and $_{{g}}\mathrm{C}_{2}={good}$ of them have two good parts. The probability is $1-\frac{{good}}{{tot}}={fr}$.

stat_quartileIqr.prompt: Arrange the data {data} in increasing order. The median of the lower half is the first quartile $Q_1$ and the median of the upper half is the third quartile $Q_3$. (If the number of data is odd, the median itself belongs to neither half.) What is the interquartile range $Q_3-Q_1$? (digits only)
hints: First rewrite the data from smallest to largest.
Split the data at the overall median into a lower and an upper half and find the median of each half.

stat_sdFreq.prompt: A frequency table has values {xs} of the variable $x$ with frequencies {fs} in that order. Treat the data as the whole population (the denominator of the variance is the total frequency). What is the standard deviation? (digits only)
hints: First find the total frequency $N$ and the mean $m=\dfrac{\sum f x}{N}$.
The variance is $\dfrac{\sum f x^2}{N}-m^2$ and the standard deviation is its positive square root.
stat_sdFreq.expl: $N={tot}$, mean $m={mean}$, $\dfrac{\sum f x^2}{N}={msq}$, so the variance is ${var}$ and the standard deviation is ${ans}$.

stat_linTransform.prompt: The variable $x$ has mean ${m}$ and variance ${vx}$. A new variable $y$ is given by $y={eq}$. What is the sum of the mean of $y$ and the variance of $y$? (digits only)
hints: If $y=ax+b$, the mean is $a\bar{x}+b$.
The variance is multiplied by $a^2$ and the added constant $b$ does not change it.
stat_linTransform.expl: The mean of $y$ is ${my}$ and its variance is ${vy}$, so the sum is ${ans}$.

stat_ciMean.prompt: A sample of {cnt} is drawn at random from a normally distributed population; the sample mean is $\bar{x}={xbar}$ and the population standard deviation is $\sigma={sig}$. The ${cl}\%$ confidence interval for the population mean is $\bar{x}-z\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\le m\le\bar{x}+z\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ with $z={z}$. What is the upper end of this interval? (digits only)
hints: First find the standard error $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$; $n$ is a perfect square so it divides evenly.
The margin of error is $z\times$(standard error); add it to $\bar{x}$ for the upper end.
stat_ciMean.expl: The standard error is $\frac{{sig}}{\sqrt{{cnt}}}={se}$, the margin of error is ${z}\times{se}={moe}$, so the upper end is ${xbar}+{moe}={ans}$.

stat_tCiLower.prompt: A sample of {cnt} from a normally distributed population has mean $\bar{x}={xbar}$ and sample standard deviation $s={sd}$. The population standard deviation is unknown, so the $t$ distribution is used; in the $t$ table for ${df}$ degrees of freedom, $P(T\le {t0})=0.975$. What is the lower end of the $95\%$ confidence interval $\bar{x}-t_0\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\le m\le\bar{x}+t_0\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$ ($t_0={t0}$) for the population mean $m$? (digits only)
hints: The degrees of freedom are $n-1$ and the standard error is $\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$.
The lower end is $\bar{x}-t_0\times$(standard error).
stat_tCiLower.expl: The standard error is $\frac{{sd}}{\sqrt{{cnt}}}={se}$, the margin of error is ${t0}\times{se}={moe}$, so the lower end is ${xbar}-{moe}={ans}$.

stat_ciProp.prompt: {cnt} people are chosen at random and asked about a policy; {ag} of them agree. With sample proportion $\hat{p}$, the ${cl}\%$ confidence interval for the population proportion is $\hat{p}-z\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}\le p\le\hat{p}+z\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}$ with $z={z}$. What is the upper end of this interval, as a number of percent? (digits only)
hints: First find the sample proportion $\hat{p}=\dfrac{{ag}}{{cnt}}$.
$\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}$ comes out rational. It is easier to work in percent.
stat_ciProp.expl: $\hat{p}={ph}\%$ and $\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{{cnt}}}={sdp}\%$, so the margin of error is ${z}\times{sdp}={moe}$ (%) and the upper end is ${ph}+{moe}={ans}$ (%).

stat_zStat.prompt: The mean lifetime of a product is known to be ${mu0}$ hours. {cnt} items made by a new process are chosen at random and their mean lifetime is $\bar{x}={xbar}$ hours. Assuming normally distributed lifetimes and an unchanged population standard deviation $\sigma={sig}$ hours, what is the value of the test statistic $Z=\dfrac{\bar{x}-{mu0}}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}$ for the null hypothesis $H_0: m={mu0}$? (digits only)
hints: Compute $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ first.
Divide the difference between the sample mean and ${mu0}$ by that value; it can be negative.

stat_rejectN.prompt: The hypotheses $H_0: m={mu0}$ and $H_1: m>{mu0}$ are tested. The population standard deviation is $\sigma={sig}$ and the sample mean is assumed to be $\bar{x}={xbar}$. The null hypothesis is rejected when the test statistic $Z=\dfrac{\bar{x}-{mu0}}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}$ is greater than ${crit}$. If the same sample mean is obtained, what is the smallest sample size $n$ (a positive integer) for which the null hypothesis is rejected? (digits only)
hints: Turn $Z>{crit}$ into an inequality for $\sqrt{n}$.
Square both sides to get the range of $n$ and take the smallest positive integer in it. Equality does not reject.
stat_rejectN.expl: From $Z=\dfrac{{xbar}-{mu0}}{{sig}}\sqrt{n}>{crit}$ we get $\sqrt{n}>{rt}$, that is $n>{lim}$ (rounded to two decimals). The smallest positive integer satisfying this is ${ans}$.

stat_stratified.prompt: A total of {ns} students are to be chosen by stratified sampling from three grades with {n1}, {n2} and {n3} students. If the sample is allocated in proportion to the size of each grade (stratum) relative to all students, how many students are chosen from the second grade? (digits only)
hints: Find the total number of students $N$ first.
The number chosen from the second grade is (total sample size)$\times\dfrac{{n2}}{N}$.
stat_stratified.expl: The total is ${pop}$ students, so ${ns}\times\dfrac{{n2}}{{pop}}={ans}$ students.

cul_pitchFifth.prompt: A reference note has frequency ${f}$ Hz. Raise it by ${k}$ octaves, then by a perfect fifth (frequency ratio $3:2$). What is the frequency of the resulting note in Hz? (digits only)
hints: One octave up doubles the frequency.
A perfect fifth up multiplies the frequency by $\frac{3}{2}$.
cul_pitchFifth.expl: Up ${k}$ octaves: ${f}\times 2^{{k}}={mid}$ Hz; a fifth higher: ${mid}\times\frac{3}{2}={ans}$ Hz.

cul_bordaTotal.prompt: A Borda count chooses among candidates A, B, C: 2 points for first place, 1 for second, 0 for third. ${n1}$ voters rank A>B>C, ${n2}$ rank B>C>A and ${n3}$ rank C>A>B. What is candidate A's total score? (digits only)
hints: First find A's place on each kind of ballot.
Add (number of voters)×(points for that place) over all ballots.
cul_bordaTotal.expl: A is first (2 points) on the first ballot, third (0) on the second and second (1) on the third: ${n1}\times2+{n2}\times0+{n3}\times1={ans}$ points.

cul_brailleCells.prompt: A braille cell has ${d}$ dot positions, each raised or not raised. Not counting the empty cell with no raised dot, how many different patterns can one cell show? (digits only)
hints: Each position has 2 states: raised or not.
Subtract the one pattern with no raised dot from all patterns.
